source: MAFF Department of Agricultural Extension / ASPIRE Project, IFAD-funded - "ដំណាំក្រូចថ្លុង" (Pomelo Cultivation Guide), 2017, 90pp
text:
The source also covers several secondary and micronutrient deficiencies recognizable by distinctive leaf patterns. Magnesium (Mg) deficiency shows as yellowing between the leaf veins on older leaves while the veins themselves stay green (an inverted V-shaped pattern of green at the leaf base), eventually leading to leaf drop; it is corrected by applying dolomite (calcium magnesium carbonate, CaMg(CO3)2) to the soil at roughly 70-150 g per tree depending on soil pH, or by a foliar spray of magnesium sulfate (MgSO4) at a dilute concentration.

Zinc (Zn) deficiency produces small, narrow, mottled yellow leaves with green veins (a pattern the source likens to a "V" shape) and shortened internodes giving a bushy, stunted look to new growth; it is treated with a foliar spray of zinc sulfate (ZnSO4). Iron (Fe) deficiency causes younger leaves to yellow strongly while veins remain green, and in severe cases leaves turn nearly white; it is linked to soil pH problems (iron becomes less available to plants in alkaline soil) and treated by correcting soil pH and/or applying iron-containing fertilizer. Calcium (Ca) deficiency and manganese (Mn) deficiency are also described, generally showing as leaf-margin or interveinal yellowing and irregular growth, both correctable through balanced fertilizing that includes these elements, guided by soil testing where possible.
